title: Common EPUB Validation Errors & Fixes (2026)
excerpt: If your EPUB looks fine in preview but still gets rejected, here's why — and how to fix the most common validation errors before you upload to KDP, Apple Books, Kobo, or IngramSpark.

html:
EPUB validation errors are a common cause of platform rejections. Your file opens fine in preview, but KDP, Apple Books, or Kobo reject it with an error message that doesn't explain what actually broke.

This guide covers the most common EPUB validation errors, what they actually mean, and how to fix each one — from the hard structural errors that block your upload to the warnings that quietly degrade your book on Kindle devices — plus why the same file can pass on one platform and fail on another.

Why Your EPUB Can Pass Preview But Still Get Rejected

Amazon's KDP Previewer and Apple Books both use their own rendering engines, and neither one runs a full EPUBCheck validation before showing you a preview. The previewer is built to display your file, not to catch every structural error in it. That's why a file can look completely normal in the previewer and still fail validation when the platform actually processes it for distribution.

The real validation happens later, using a much stricter set of rules — and different platforms enforce those rules differently. Understanding this gap is the first step to avoiding rejected uploads.

Hard Errors vs Warnings

Validation feedback splits into two categories, and the difference decides how urgently you need to act.

Hard errors block publication entirely. The file will not go live until you fix them and re-upload. These include a broken package structure, a missing table of contents, invalid XML, and missing required metadata. KDP usually flags these within minutes of upload.

Warnings don't block publication, but they degrade the reading experience — deprecated HTML tags, unsupported CSS, and oversized images. The book publishes, but readers may see formatting problems on certain devices, especially older e-ink hardware. Fix every hard error first, then work through warnings, starting with the ones most likely to affect visible layout.

Hard Error: Broken EPUB Package Structure

A typical message looks like:

"The file structure of your EPUB is invalid. The mimetype
 file is missing or incorrectly compressed."

What it means: An EPUB is a ZIP archive with strict rules. The mimetype file must be the very first entry and stored uncompressed, META-INF/container.xml must point to a real OPF package document, and only the contents — not the top-level folder — belong in the archive. This breaks most often when authors rename a .zip to .epub, or when a ZIP tool compresses the mimetype by default.

How to fix it: Repackage with an EPUB-aware tool. If you do it by hand, add the mimetype file first using the store (no-compression) method, then add everything else. Run the result through the free EPUB Validator to confirm the package structure passes before re-uploading.

Hard Error: Missing Navigation Document or TOC

This is one of the most common EPUB 3 errors, and it usually shows up as something like:

oebps/content.opf: error while parsing file: exactly one manifest item must declare the 'nav' property (number of 'nav' items: 0)

What it means: Every EPUB 3 file needs a navigation document — a special XHTML file that acts as your table of contents and is explicitly marked as the nav item inside the OPF manifest. EPUB 2 files use an NCX file for the same job. If this declaration is missing, empty, or was stripped during conversion, the file either fails validation immediately or publishes with a table of contents readers can't use.

How to fix it: Open your OPF file and check the manifest for an item with properties="nav". If it's missing, add the nav property to your existing TOC file's manifest entry, or rebuild one. The TOC Generator can produce a valid navigation document from your chapter headings when yours is missing or broken. This is one of the most common issues when a Word-to-EPUB conversion doesn't handle the table of contents correctly.

Hard Error: Duplicate IDs in the Manifest or Spine

Another frequent issue is duplicate id attributes across manifest items or spine references. EPUB requires every ID inside the file to be unique — even across different XML files that reference the OPF.

What it means: Somewhere in the conversion process, two elements ended up with the same identifier. This often happens when chapters are merged, split, or reordered without updating their internal references.

How to fix it: Run the file through a validator that flags exact ID locations, then rename the duplicate. If you're editing by hand, search the entire OPF and each XHTML file for the conflicting ID string to make sure you catch every reference to it.

Hard Error: Malformed OPF Manifest

A representative message:

"One or more files referenced in the manifest do not exist."

"The OPF spine references an item ID that is not defined
 in the manifest."

What it means: The OPF file lists every component of your EPUB. If a file in the manifest doesn't exist, if a file that exists isn't listed, or if a spine reference points to an ID the manifest never defines, the platform flags a structural error. Renaming or moving a chapter after export is the usual trigger.

How to fix it: Compare the manifest item list against the actual files in your EPUB folder. Remove entries for files that no longer exist, add entries for files that do, and confirm every spine idref matches a manifest id. File paths are case-sensitive — Images/Photo.jpg and images/photo.jpg are different files on the Linux servers the stores run.

Hard Error: Invalid XML in Chapter Files

A representative message:

"One or more content files contain invalid XML. Check your
 XHTML files for unclosed tags or improperly escaped characters."

What it means: EPUB chapter files are XHTML — strict XML, not forgiving HTML. A single malformed element fails the entire file. The most common violations:

  • Bare & in text or URLs — it must be written as &
  • Unclosed void elements: <br> and <img> must self-close as <br/> and <img .../>
  • Attribute values without quotes: <p align=center> instead of <p align="center">
  • Overlapping tags: <b><i>text</b></i> must close in reverse order
  • Double dashes inside HTML comments (<!-- -- --> is invalid XML)

How to fix it: Run your EPUB through the EPUB Validator — it lists every XML error by filename and line number. Fix each one in a text editor. If the errors are widespread across many files, rebuilding from the manuscript with Full Manuscript Mode is faster than patching hundreds of individual errors by hand.

Hard Error: Missing or Invalid Metadata

A representative message:

"Your EPUB file is missing required metadata. Please ensure
 your file includes a title, author, and language."

"The language code is not valid. Use a BCP 47 tag such as
 'en' or 'en-US'."

What it means: The OPF must contain a unique identifier (ISBN or UUID), dc:title, dc:creator, and dc:language in valid BCP 47 format. Missing fields or invalid values cause rejection. The single most common mistake is setting dc:language to the word "English" instead of the code en.

How to fix it: Open your OPF and verify each required element is present and correctly formatted. The Metadata Builder generates properly formatted OPF metadata you can paste straight into your package file, with no format guessing.

Hard Error: Image Problems

A representative message:

"One or more images referenced in your book were not found
 in the EPUB package."

"Image format not supported. Use JPEG, PNG, GIF, or SVG."

What it means: Stores reject EPUBs that reference images missing from the package, and they reject unsupported formats — EPUB supports JPEG, PNG, GIF, and SVG, but not WEBP. A wrong relative path is a common trigger: if your chapter file lives in OEBPS/Text/ and your image in OEBPS/Images/, the path must be ../Images/cover.jpg, not Images/cover.jpg.

How to fix it: Validate to get a list of broken image references, fix the paths in your HTML, and convert WEBP or other unsupported formats to JPEG or PNG. Make sure every referenced image is included in the package and declared in the OPF manifest with the correct media type. For covers, the Cover Checker verifies dimensions, format, and color mode before you embed or upload.

Hard Error: DRM or Encryption Conflicts

A representative message:

"Your file appears to be DRM-protected and cannot be published.
 Please upload an unprotected version of your book."

What it means: A file that was previously DRM-protected by another platform can't be published. EPUBs downloaded from Kobo, Google Play, or Apple Books are DRM-locked, and a copy you download as a buyer from KDP carries KDP's own DRM — none of them can be re-uploaded.

How to fix it: Always publish from your original EPUB source — the file you created or received from your formatter, never one downloaded from a retail store. If you've lost the original, rebuild it from your manuscript with Full Manuscript Mode.

Hard Error: Embedded Font Problems

A representative message:

"Your EPUB contains embedded fonts that are not properly
 declared in the package manifest."

What it means: Embedded fonts are allowed, but they must be declared in the OPF manifest with the correct media type, and they must carry a license that permits embedding. Commercial fonts from services like Adobe Fonts often don't permit ebook embedding, which can trigger a content rejection.

How to fix it: Use only fonts whose license explicitly allows embedding — the SIL Open Font License is the safe choice. Declare each font in the manifest with media-type="application/vnd.ms-opentype" for OTF/TTF or application/font-woff for WOFF. If you're unsure a font's license permits embedding, drop it and reference system fonts through a CSS font-family stack instead.

Ghost Spacing and Silent Rendering Problems

This one is sneaky because it's often invisible until a specific device or storefront tries to render it. Ghost spacing usually comes from leftover empty paragraph tags, non-breaking spaces, or inconsistent line breaks carried over from a Word export.

What it means: Your file technically validates, but the reading experience is broken — awkward gaps between paragraphs, inconsistent spacing before headings, or unexpected blank pages. KDP might accept a file with ghost spacing because its validation is more forgiving, while Apple Books or Kobo enforce stricter formatting checks and either reject the file or flag it during review.

How to fix it: Clean up leftover empty tags and non-breaking space characters directly in the HTML/XHTML source, not just in the visual editor. This is exactly the kind of issue that passing one platform's check doesn't guarantee against another's — always test your file across multiple validators, not just the one your target platform provides.

Warnings That Don't Block Upload

Warnings publish your book but leave formatting problems behind. The three you'll see most often:

Unsupported CSS properties. Kindle devices ignore properties like text-shadow, box-shadow, border-radius, position: fixed, certain flexbox rules, and CSS animations — especially on older hardware. The style is dropped, which can shift your layout. Use fallback-safe CSS: padding for visual separation instead of box-shadow, margins instead of position-based layout.

Deprecated HTML tags. Tags like <font>, <center>, and presentational <b>/<i> generate warnings and may break on future firmware. Replace them with <strong>, <em>, and text alignment in your CSS file.

Image resolution and size. KDP recommends roughly 96 DPI for interior images and at least 1600px on the long side for covers. Print-resolution 300 DPI images bloat the file without improving screen quality and slow rendering on older Kindles. Resize and compress interior images before embedding.

Platform-by-Platform: Why the Same File Behaves Differently

PlatformValidation strictnessCommon failure point
Amazon KDPMore forgivingMissing nav property, broken TOC links
Apple BooksStricterGhost spacing, manifest metadata gaps
KoboModerateCover image embedding, CSS compatibility
IngramSparkStrictestAny EPUBCheck error at all — no tolerance

If you're publishing across multiple platforms, the safest approach is to build for IngramSpark's strict standard first. A file clean enough to pass there will almost always pass everywhere else — including KDP, Apple Books, and Kobo.

How to Validate Before You Upload

Before submitting to any platform, run your EPUB through a validator that checks structure, metadata, and manifest integrity — not just visual formatting. Look for:

  • A clean pass with zero EPUBCheck errors, not just "no visible issues"
  • A properly declared nav document and a working table of contents
  • No duplicate IDs across the manifest or spine
  • Valid, complete metadata — identifier, title, creator, and a BCP 47 language code
  • No leftover empty tags or spacing artifacts from your original Word or Google Docs export

A few habits make this reliable:

  • Fix everything before each re-upload. Don't upload again until the validator shows zero errors — repeated failed uploads on the same title can slow your KDP review queue.
  • Save the validator report first. If you introduce a new error while fixing an old one, the saved report tells you what changed.
  • Finish in Kindle Previewer. Validation catches structural errors; Previewer catches visual problems. Check the TOC menu and image display on at least a phone and an e-ink device.
  • Keep your source manuscript clean. Most EPUB errors originate upstream. Run the Word Cleanup Checker on every manuscript before conversion — fixing at the source is always faster than patching after.

Frequently Asked Questions

How long does KDP take to process an EPUB after upload?

Structural errors are flagged within minutes. If your rejection arrives in the first few minutes, it's a structural or format problem you fix before the file enters content review. Content review — for policy compliance — takes 24–72 hours, and a file that passes structural validation enters it automatically.

How do I know if my rejection is technical or content-related?

Technical rejections appear within minutes and cite file structure, format, metadata, or images. Content rejections appear after 24–72 hours and cite policy (prohibited content, misleading metadata, copyright). Under 10 minutes means a technical problem an EPUB validator report will pinpoint.

Can I use EPUB 2 for KDP?

Yes, KDP accepts EPUB 2. But EPUB 3 is the current standard, supports more Kindle features, and triggers fewer warnings. For a new file, target EPUB 3 from the start; for an old EPUB 2 file that keeps failing, rebuilding to EPUB 3 is often faster than fixing every legacy issue.

My EPUB worked on KDP before — why is it being rejected now?

KDP periodically tightens its validation. A file that passed a year ago can fail today under stricter parsing or new accessibility checks. Run it through a current validator to see which previously-tolerated issues are now flagged.

Can I fix EPUB errors without specialized software?

Yes. EPUB files are ZIP archives of HTML, CSS, and XML. Unzip, fix the flagged file in any text editor, repackage correctly, and you're done. The hard part is knowing which file and what to change — which is exactly what a validator report gives you, with filename and line number.

Will fixing errors on an already-published book affect sales or ranking?

No. Uploading a corrected version doesn't affect sales history, reviews, or ranking. Existing readers get the update automatically via Whispersync, usually within 24–48 hours. You can update as often as you need with no penalty.
